title: Valid Parentheses: stack matching pairs.
keyPoints: Push every opening bracket and on each closer pop the top and verify it is the matching opener.
Two failure conditions: empty stack on a closer (unmatched close), and non-empty stack after the scan (unmatched open).
Use a Map from closer to expected opener for clean, extensible matching logic.
Time is O(n) because each character is pushed and popped at most once; space is O(n) worst case.
Prefer ArrayDeque over the legacy Stack class for the internal stack.
A string of odd length can never be balanced, so reject it in O(1) as an early exit.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, and on every closer pop the top and check it matches; the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Valid Parentheses** – a classic stack problem that checks whether every opening bracket has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket.
- **Algorithm** – push each opening bracket onto a stack, and on each closing bracket pop the top and verify it is the matching opener type.
- **Two failure conditions** – an empty stack when a closer arrives means an unmatched close, and a non-empty stack after the full scan means unmatched opens.
- **Matching map** – a small Map from each closer to its expected opener keeps the comparison clean and easy to extend.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time because each character is pushed and popped at most once, and O(n) space in the worst case of all openers.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh at the National Bank of India opening nested approval requests. He opens a loan request, then inside it opens a document-verification request, then inside that a signature request. Each request he opens, he writes on a sticky note and places on top of a pile. When a request closes, the one on top must be the most recently opened. If a signature request tries to close while a document request is on top, the paperwork is out of order and the batch is rejected.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Validation of "{[()]}"
  ──────────────────────

  Index 0: '{' → push
  Stack: [ { ]

  Index 1: '[' → push
  Stack: [ [  { ]

  Index 2: '(' → push
  Stack: [ (  [  { ]

  Index 3: ')' → pop '(' matches ')' ✓
  Stack: [ [  { ]

  Index 4: ']' → pop '[' matches ']' ✓
  Stack: [ { ]

  Index 5: '}' → pop '{' matches '}' ✓
  Stack: [ ] (empty)

  Result: stack is empty → VALID
```

```text
  Failure on "({)}"
  ─────────────────

  Index 0: '(' → push
  Stack: [ ( ]

  Index 1: '{' → push
  Stack: [ {  ( ]

  Index 2: ')' → pop '{' does NOT match ')' ✗
  Result: MISMATCH → INVALID
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parentheses is the textbook example of when a stack is the right data structure, because the rule governing brackets is Last In First Out: the bracket that closes must always be the one most recently opened. My approach is to scan the string once, push every opening bracket onto a stack, and on every closing bracket pop the top and confirm it is the matching opener. I keep a small map from each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket so the match check is a constant-time lookup rather than a chain of conditionals.

There are two failure cases I handle explicitly. The first is a closing bracket arriving when the stack is empty, which means a closer has no matching opener. The second is the string ending with brackets still on the stack, which means some openers were never closed. Both checks together are what make the solution correct, and candidates who forget the final `isEmpty()` check wrongly pass strings like three open parentheses.

The algorithm runs in O(n) time because each character is pushed and popped at most once, and it uses O(n) space in the worst case of an all-opening string. I always reach for `ArrayDeque` rather than the old `Stack` class, because `Stack` extends `Vector` and synchronizes every call, which adds pointless locking in a single-threaded parser. I also add the odd-length shortcut: a string of odd length can never be balanced, so I reject it in constant time before the loop even starts.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this as a fast pre-check on fee-calculation formulas whose nested segments are delimited by brackets. A malformed formula with crossed or dangling brackets gets rejected before the parser ever evaluates it, which protects the calculation engine from corrupt expressions and gives the operations team a clean audit trail of every rejected formula.

Remember one sentence: push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
